title: Prego Roll
author: Chef Manuel
desc: Rump seared hard and rested, piled onto toasted bread spread with onion marmalade, with a garlic, chilli, red wine and tomato sauce spooned over — twenty-five minutes from start to finish.
longDesc: Prego means nail in Portuguese, and the name refers to the garlic studded into the steak. It arrived in South Africa through the Portuguese-Mozambican community and is now on every roadhouse and pub menu in the country. The whole dish turns on two things: not overcooking the steak, and toasting the bread so it can take the sauce without collapsing. It is a fast dish and it is at its best made to order.
ingredients: 1 tbsp olive oil, for the pan
1 French loaf, cut into thick slices
equipment: Griddle pan or toaster, for the bread
steps: Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil with the red wine, crushed garlic and chopped chilli in a saucepan over high heat.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook for 10 minutes, until the sauce starts to thicken. Season.

Meanwhile heat the remaining 1 tbsp of oil in a large pan and sear the steaks until well browned on both sides — no more than 2 minutes on the first side and no more than 4 on the second, depending on thickness and how you want them.
Rest the steaks on a board for a few minutes, then slice them.
Toast the slices of French loaf in a hot pan, under the grill or in a toaster until golden, and spread them with the onion marmalade.
Top with the sliced steak and a generous spoonful of the prego sauce.
chefTips: Rest the steak before slicing, even for a few minutes. Sliced straight from the pan it loses its juice onto the board rather than into the bread.
Toast the bread properly. Untoasted bread under this sauce is soggy before it reaches the table.
Two minutes and then four, no more. These are steaks in a roll, not a braise.
A spoonful of peri-peri in the sauce is the common South African addition and makes it a peri-peri prego.
The onion marmalade is optional but it is what balances the chilli and the wine.
commonMistakes: Overcooking the steak, which is the only real failure here.
Slicing it straight out of the pan.
Reducing the sauce too far, so it becomes a paste rather than something that soaks in.
storage: Not a keeping dish. The sauce keeps 3 days refrigerated.
reheating: Reheat the sauce and cook fresh steak.
healthBenefits: Rump is a lean, high-protein cut with iron, zinc and B12.
The sauce is tomato, garlic and chilli rather than cream or butter.
A quick cook, so very little added fat.
culturalNote: The prego is ubiquitous in South Africa and almost nobody thinks of it as Portuguese any more, which is a reasonable measure of how completely this strand has been absorbed. The Madeiran espetada — garlic and bay beef on a long skewer — travelled the same route and is still recognisably foreign; the prego is not.
